name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: The Pa. budget included additional funding for a handful of school districts for third year in a row
description: For the third year in a row, the annual state budget included provisions that sent additional dollars to a handful of school districts, outside of the typical funding formulas that govern state support for the 500 public school districts.
text:
The state Capitol building in Harrisburg. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)For the third year in a row, the annual state budget included provisions that sent additional dollars to a handful of school districts, outside of the typical funding formulas that govern state support for the 500 public school districts. 
And for the third year in a row, all of those districts are represented by Democrats in the state House.
Collectively, four school districts are set to receive $8 million in the 2026-2027 school year, on top of what they receive through the commonwealth’s basic education formula and newer adequacy formula. 
That’s on top of $5 million that went to a school district represented by House Speaker Joanna McClinton (D-Philadelphia) last year, and a tweak to the adequacy formula that sent $14 million to 11 school districts in the 2024-2025 budget.
But the four districts all faced unique financial challenges. Democratic lawmakers who sought the funding bumps in the latest budget say it was a product of those needs and their advocacy, not partisan favoritism.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
A spokesperson for House Democrats did not respond to requests for comment.
When asked whether he advocated for similar funding bumps for struggling school districts represented by Republicans, House Minority Leader Jesse Topper (R-Bedford) told the Capital-Star “that’s not something that we normally look at.”
“There are always those kind of provisions that are inserted [in the budget],” he continued. “That’s not something I want to see. I want to redo the entire way we fund education and the adequacy formula. I’m not thrilled with any of them.”
The repeated inclusion of additional funds for certain districts raises questions about the effectiveness of Pennsylvania’s formulas for funding its public schools, and about whether all parts of the state are able to access additional funds when necessary.
“I don’t think that there is a perfect formula out there that fits all,” said Edward Albert, the executive director of the Pennsylvania Association of Rural and Small School Districts. 
While he praised the additional funding some schools have received through the new adequacy formula — the result of a 2023 court decision that found Pennsylvania’s school funding formula was unconstitutionally inequitable — he acknowledged that there are some district leaders who have felt left behind by it.
School bus parked in Upper Burrell Township, Westmoreland County on Jan. 16, 2026. (Photo by John Beale for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“We’re rejoicing this year with what we got in the budget, but I have superintendents emailing me saying, ‘I didn’t get anything,’” he said.
But Albert doesn’t see the apparent partisan divide over which school districts are receiving supplemental funding as necessarily a show of favoritism, even if the rural school districts he works with are more likely to be represented by Republicans.
“If you’re just looking at the bigger picture from 30,000 feet up, Democrats are obviously gonna want more money, and obviously Republicans are a little more conservative,” he said. “The whole thing is not black and white.”
Difficult decisions
The Muhlenberg School District in Berks County faced a $2 million budget shortfall in the 2025-2026 school year, leading officials to mull staff cuts and a property tax hike.
In this year’s state budget, the district represented by Rep. Jacklyn Rusnock (D-Berks) received $2.5 million in additional funds, on top of what it was set to receive from the basic education funding formula and the newer adequacy formula.
“Muhlenberg is the fastest growing school district in Berks County, “Rusnock said. “It’s growing exponentially faster than every other district.”
According to Rusnock, that’s caused a unique financial strain that the school funding formula is not adept at keeping up with. So she went to legislative leaders and asked for help.
“The way I look at it, we’re bringing in additional funding that focuses on the district’s needs, and it’s also not placing an additional burden on the local taxpayers,” she said. “This is something that I’ve been working with leadership on since December.”
Asked about why she thinks only school districts represented by House Democrats have received additional funding outside the formulas in recent years, she said it wasn’t something she’d considered.
“I didn’t realize that had happened,” she said. “I can only speak for myself. I am an advocate of public education. I’m a product of education. I taught in the public education system. I just think it’s really important our school districts are getting what they need … I really can’t speak to why it would be a Democrat or Republican issue.”
The Steelton-Highspire School District in the Harrisburg area in Dauphin County faced a $4.5 million budget shortfall, leading to discussions about cutting dozens of staff. Along with basic education and adequacy funding, Steelton-Highspire will receive $1 million in additional funding after lawmakers pushed for more help.
According to Rep. Dave Madsen (D-Dauphin), who represents the district, the idling of the Cleveland Cliffs steel mill in Steelton, which employed roughly 500 people, strained the community’s tax base. As it stands, it’s not clear what can replace the hundred of lost jobs or the business itself.
“It is a very unique situation when you have such a small population that has the conditions they have in terms of their tax base,” he said. “I don’t see how they could overcome it without some sort of additional help, and that was the case I made to leadership.”
Asked if he thought partisanship played into Steelton-Highspire being awarded money outside the typical school funding formulas, Madsen couldn’t say.
“I advocate for my district, and I know other colleagues, both Republican and Democrat, have similar circumstances. What their conversations with leadership look like, I’m not privy to. I just know with the ones that I had, working with my school district, we just laid out a case for why we would need additional help.”
The Morrisville-Borough School District in Bucks County is set to get $3.5 million in the 2026-2027 school year outside the typical funding formulas.
Rep. Jim Prokopiak (D-Bucks) described issues not entirely dissimilar from those Steelton-Highspire faced.
“Fifty years ago, there was a lot of industry that was attached to the school district. As industries eroded, the tax bases eroded,” he said. “The money for Morrisville this year was correcting a problem that had been decades in the making.”
Years of funding struggles led the school district to take on debt.

Asked about the political tilt of the awards, Prokopiak pointed to issues that have primarily affected suburban and urban school districts, which are more likely to be represented by Democrats.
Pennsylvania has a school funding policy known as hold harmless, which ensures that, even if student population declines, schools continue to receive the same amount of money from the state that they did the year before.
“I don’t think it’s a party situation. I think it’s more demographic changes,” Prokopiak said. “Rural school districts have traditionally, because of the population decreases in those areas, actually gotten more funding than they necessarily would under a new formula. Many counties in Pennsylvania are shrinking, but they still maintain their same funding formula. Areas that are growing tend to be more in the suburban areas, which recently have tended to be more represented by Democrats than Republicans.”
The Whitehall-Coplay School District in Lehigh County is also set to receive $1 million, but Rep. Jeanne McNeill (D-Lehigh), who represents it, did not respond to a request for comment from the Capital-Star.
Like the other school districts, it faced a multimillion dollar budget deficit and officials mulled difficult decisions like whether to cut staff.
How it’s played out in recent years
Last year only one district, the William Penn school fistrict in Delaware County, received an additional funding bump. It had struggled financially for years and was one of six named plaintiffs in the adequacy funding lawsuit – which led to a new formula being created in 2024. 
William Penn is in House Speaker McClinton’s district. 
State budget sent $5 million to a struggling school district represented by the Pa. House speaker

At the time, a spokesperson for House Democrats told the Capital-Star, “the guiding principle for the House Democratic caucus has always been and always will be to help the least advantaged. There is an overlap to the extent that our leaders represent some of the poorest areas. Maybe that is a good thing.”
During negotiations over the 2024-2025 state budget, 11 school districts were singled out to receive annual budget bumps of $14 million collectively, including William Penn and Steelton-Highspire.
Like all the five school districts that received supplemental funding in the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 budget, all 11 were all represented by Democrats in the state House.
But lawmakers and experts told the Capital-Star that year that the selection of schools in Democratic lawmakers’ districts was the result of tense negotiations over the creation of the adequacy formula.
When creating the new adequacy formula to address the school funding lawsuit, lawmakers in both parties knew that it needed to increase funding for school districts in impoverished areas. But there was disagreement over how that should be measured.

Eleven Pennsylvania school districts got $14 million in extra funding in the latest budget


Democrats advocated for a formula that would measure local poverty based on figures collected by school districts themselves. They argued those numbers were the most accurate available since the district staff  collecting them regularly interacted with, and were likely to be trusted by, impacted families. 
Republicans preferred data collected in annual surveys by the U.S. Census Bureau, arguing that school districts may be incentivized to meddle with data that would affect their own funding.
It was a fight that Republicans ultimately won. But that meant dozens of school districts receiving less funding than they would have under the Democrat-backed plan. 
The additional funding for 11 school districts was a way to bridge that gap for some of those most affected by the change. They were also represented by Democratic lawmakers who plead for additional help ahead of an expectedly close vote over the implementation of the adequacy formula.
Albert, the executive director of the Pennsylvania Association of Rural and Small School Districts, suggests one way lawmakers could help districts that fall under unique strain would be to build funding for them into the budget.
“Maybe there’s a pool of money put off to the side to kind of offset those to make it right,” he said. 
The hope is that the funding being readily available would make lawmakers of both parties more willing to advocate for it reaching school districts they represent.
Albert also advocated for increased transparency and accountability measures to ensure that school districts are using state funding to boost educational outcomes. He hopes that would make lawmakers less reticent to provide additional funding for struggling school districts.
“I’m a firm believer in accountability. I think when we’re asking for money, I think it’s very important for us to say, ‘here’s what we’re using the money for.’ … But that’s a two way street. I think legislators should want to come to schools.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Court: Minneapolis schools can keep providing layoff protection to teachers of color
description: A federal judge has dismissed a U.S. Department of Justice lawsuit targeting a Minneapolis Public Schools policy that shields teachers of color from seniority-based layoffs. In his ruling Monday, U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz wrote that the policy — adopted in 2022 to help end a 14-day Minneapolis Federation of Teachers strike — does raise […]
text:
(Photo by Will Jacott/Minnesota Reformer)A federal judge has dismissed a U.S. Department of Justice lawsuit targeting a Minneapolis Public Schools policy that shields teachers of color from seniority-based layoffs.
In his ruling Monday, U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz wrote that the policy — adopted in 2022 to help end a 14-day Minneapolis Federation of Teachers strike — does raise concerns about the “legality of the racial discrimination in which MPS is forced to engage.” The lawsuit cannot proceed, however, without the teachers union — which was left off the list of defendants when the Trump administration sued the district in December. 
The policy ended typical last-in, first-out rules for teachers from underrepresented backgrounds in an effort to improve recruitment and retention in one of the state’s most diverse districts. It was adopted by MPS as part of a collective bargaining agreement, making the union a necessary party to the federal government’s lawsuit. The problem for the Trump administration: DOJ can only bring cases alleging discrimination against government entities. Labor unions, like the MFT, are private. 
Schiltz said proceeding without the union would leave MPS in an “untenable position” as it chooses to violate either a federal injunction or its own collective bargaining agreement with the teachers unions. 
“MPS and the union sit on opposite sides of the bargaining table, and the court cannot simply trust that one party to a (collective bargaining agreement) will safeguard the interests of the other party,” Schiltz wrote. 
The teachers union pushed for layoff protections in 2022 because teachers of color tend to be younger and disproportionately affected by last-in, first-out downsizing. Around 20% of Minneapolis teachers are people of color, compared to two-thirds of their students. The policy requires the district to skip over staff members from “underrepresented populations” during seniority-based layoffs or involuntary reassignments. Laid-off teachers from underrepresented groups must also be the first to be reinstated if called back. 
The policy doesn’t explicitly mention race to help withstand legal challenges.
Minneapolis Public Schools praised Schiltz’s order in a statement to the Reformer.
“Minneapolis Public Schools is pleased the Court granted our motion to dismiss this case. We remain committed to working with our labor partners to ensure collective bargaining agreements are in the best interest of our students and employees.”
Marcia Howard, president of the teachers union, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
The Trump administration alleged the MPS policy was discriminatory after the school district defended the same policy in another lawsuit by a local resident. Deborah Clapp, with the backing of conservative legal foundation Judicial Watch, argued that she was harmed as a taxpayer for funding a discriminatory policy. (A judge tossed the case in January of 2025.)
Schiltz said teachers who wish to challenge the policy can file a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which can pursue cases against private entities.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Democratic gubernatorial candidates split on education; advocates see next year as pivotal
description: Amy Starzecki, administrator of the Superior school district in northern Wisconsin, detailed the financial difficulties her district has faced in recent years to a roomful of public education advocates gathered in the auditorium of Superior High School at the end of July. Starzecki’s district had to transfer $6 million from its general fund to cover […]
text:
Former DOA Secretary Joel Brennan, who is running in the Democratic primary for governor, speaks with State Superintendent Jill Underly at the Wisconsin Public Education Network summit in Superior. Underly told the Wisconsin Examiner that school voucher programs are a “drain on our public education system,” but cannot be shut down overnight. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Amy Starzecki, administrator of the Superior school district in northern Wisconsin, detailed the financial difficulties her district has faced in recent years to a roomful of public education advocates gathered in the auditorium of Superior High School at the end of July.
Starzecki’s district had to transfer $6 million from its general fund to cover special education expenses that aren’t reimbursed by the state, she said, while at the same time coping with a 40% increase in healthcare costs. She said she was grateful that the community passed a referendum two years ago to help with costs, but it expires in 2029.
“I’m very nervous about whether we continue to push forward another referendum or whether it will pass, recognizing there’s fatigue in all of our communities and our families are experiencing the same inflation,” Starzecki said, adding that the school has taken steps to cut costs by closing a middle school and reducing administrative overhead. 
“We feel very strongly that we need to be looking at the funding formula and making sure that we are addressing the increased inflationary costs and increasing the revenue tied to that so that we don’t have to go to referendum and close that gap,” Starzecki said. “We need to have a significant change in our special education reimbursement to stop from pulling from our operating budget in order to cover the cost of those expenses that those students need.”
Public education advocates have for years called on the Republican-led Legislature to significantly boost state aid to public schools. 
The calls have gone unanswered by lawmakers, including this year when schools received no increase in their general aid from the state. But advocates see an opening for change with voters choosing both a new governor and electing candidates who will determine which party  controls the state Senate and Assembly next year, along with a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of  the state’s school funding formula. A favorable decision for the plaintiffs in the lawsuit could require an overhaul of the formula by the Legislature and the new governor. 
Democrats competing in the primary  for governor, including Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan, state Sen. Kelda Roys and state Rep. Francesca Hong, participated in a forum in Superior during the annual Wisconsin Public Education Network summer summit at the end of July. Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who is also running, did not take part, nor did Republican candidates U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and Andy Manske. 
All the Democratic candidates for governor have said they support increasing funding for the state’s public schools, raising the amount the state pays for special education and restoring the state’s guarantee to cover two-thirds of school costs. (Crowley, Hong and Roys have promised to work toward  a 90% special education reimbursement rate from the state, while Brennan has said that 60% is the “the most reasonable” rate for the state to adopt immediately.)
Tiffany has also said he would increase school funding, including for special education, while cutting property taxes, including by overturning Evers’ 400-year veto of a measure capping school districts’ ability to raise revenue from local property taxpayers. He has not laid out a specific plan for both increasing funding for schools and cutting taxes. Tiffany has also supported school choice programs, including the Trump administration’s federal tax credit program rewarding people who donate money to school choice programs. 
Manske recently said on social media that he supports universal school choice because he doesn’t “like parents/kids being robbed of choices for education” but that he is also interested in reforms to ensure all schools follow the same rules. 
The Democrats diverge on how they say they will handle Wisconsin’s school choice programs, which allow students to attend private schools and independent charter schools using taxpayer funds. 
Brennan and Crowley want focus on public growth, not cutting vouchers
Brennan and Crowley have said they want additional transparency and accountability measures put in place for voucher schools, but have not proposed any plans to sunset the programs
Crowley has argued that the state first needs to strengthen public schools before considering whether the voucher system should change. He has said he would not expand or shrink the programs, including the Milwaukee and statewide choice programs.
Public education advocates have for years called on the Republican-led Legislature to significantly boost state aid to public schools. Democratic candidates for governor attended the WPEN summit in July. Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley was absent, along with Republican candidates Tom Tiffany and Andy Manske. Summit organizers put place cards by their empty chairs. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Instead, his campaign says, he will focus on investing in and improving the state’s public schools. His campaign told the Wisconsin Examiner that “his priority is ensuring public schools are fully funded and prepared to serve every student, including if and when the state’s voucher programs eventually sunset.” 
Crowley has explained this stance by saying that the state’s public schools would not be prepared for the influx of students that would arrive if voucher schools shut down immediately. He recently said on an episode of Pod Save America that candidates who say they will end the programs are not “being honest or realistic about the situation.” 
“This is going to upend, not just these children’s learning, their families, but what will this actually do to the public school system?” Crowley said. “We just did a $250 million referendum to make sure we have enough resources for [Milwaukee public schools] students. How are we going to send 30,000 [additional] students to the public schools?”
According to the Department of Public Instruction, the state’s school voucher system, which includes the Milwaukee, Racine, statewide and special needs programs, cost over $700 million in taxpayer dollars this year, with more than 60,000 students participating.
About 30,000 students use vouchers through the Milwaukee Parental Choice Program to attend private schools or independent charter schools. The cost of the Milwaukee program, which is paid for through state general purpose revenue, has grown to over $300 million. When the Milwaukee program launched as a small pilot program in 1990, it cost $700,000.
Crowley’s campaign told the Examiner that he would make increasing funding for public education his top priority “by directing available state resources toward K-12 education before pursuing additional tax cuts or other spending priorities.” 
“David does not see this as a choice between maintaining the current voucher system and strengthening public schools,” a campaign spokesperson said. “Rather than expanding voucher programs, he would prioritize new education investments in public schools, including increased general school aid and higher special education reimbursement, while maintaining the current voucher programs without expansion.” 
Brennan has also made the argument that it’s not feasible to suddenly end Wisconsin’s school voucher programs, especially in Milwaukee. During the only televised debate in the primary he said he supports capping enrollment in the programs and disclosing the cost of private voucher schools on taxpayers’ property tax bills. 
“There are representatives in Milwaukee… for whom more than half the people who live there are sending their kids to private schools. We have to live in the real world. This is dividing Democrats,” Brennan said at the debate. “I wouldn’t put legislators in a position where they’re going to have to tell parents that they can’t send their kids to their schools of their choice.”
Colleston Morgan, the executive director of the City Forward Collective, a Milwaukee-based education advocacy group that supports school choice, has called for Democrats to embrace school vouchers and private-school choice.
Morgan noted that, especially in Milwaukee many Black and Latino families rely on school vouchers, saying it’s too late to backtrack. 
The Milwaukee program, Morgan said in an interview with the Examiner, has been championed by Black public officials, including former Milwaukee Superintendent Howard Fuller and  Polly Williams, a Democratic state lawmaker, and was designed to serve Black and Hispanic families seeking an alternative to the Milwaukee Public Schools. Fuller has expressed reservations about the program’s expansion, however, saying he does not support universal school choice.
“I think we have forgotten that history in the current political moment, but I also think we have forgotten the reality that when you say we’re going to end vouchers or we’re going to put forward budget amendments that exclude the voucher program from these increases — what you’re saying is you’re defunding or underfunding one-fourth of the students in the state’s largest city,” Morgan said. “That it is a position — it’s incompatible to me with our values as Democrats.”
Morgan’s organization has not endorsed a candidate, but was complimentary of Evers, who has overseen the largest boost in funding for school choice programs in Wisconsin state history while negotiating budgets with Republicans.
“I would like to see leadership in the governor’s office that continues that legacy,” Morgan said.
Hong and Roys propose sunsetting vouchers
Hong and Roys both support sunsetting the state’s voucher programs, but have proposed different timelines for phasing them out. 
Advocates have acknowledged that the phase-out would likely not be quick, including Department of Public Instruction Superintendent Jill Underly. She said the voucher programs are a “drain on our public education system,” but cannot be shut down overnight.
“We don’t want to disrupt kids’ lives, so you come up with a responsible plan,” Underly said. She noted that the state has ended programs before, including Chapter 220 in Milwaukee, a program that allowed Black students in the city to attend suburban schools as part of an integration an effort. The program was phased out in 2015.
Underly, a Democrat who hasn’t endorsed a candidate in the gubernatorial primary and noted that her office is nominally nonpartisan, has said she will be prepared to knock on doors for pro-public school candidates after the primary.
Underly also said she plans to “swing for the fences” with her agency’s request in the next state budget. In its 2024 request, DPI requested at least $3 billion in additional spending for Wisconsin schools. Underly said she saw each candidate explaining “how they would re-prioritize public education within the revenue that they have.”
“We do have a limited amount of money or revenue, but it’s about priorities,” Underly said.
Holly Sweeney, a school board member from Elk Mound,  said she is concerned about the amount of money that goes to vouchers in her area — about $120,000 —  which, she said, “doesn’t sound like a lot, but for our little school district, that’s a lot.” (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Roys and Hong, who are both Madison-area state lawmakers, have campaigned on the pledge that they will direct public money to public schools. 
Roys, who calls herself the “public education candidate” and has said if elected, she would dedicate the state’s entire projected budget surplus to public schools and seek to sunset the state’s voucher program. 
Roys has laid out a three-step approach to sunsetting the private school voucher system. Those steps include putting in place additional transparency and accountability measures, ending the statewide program in the next state budget and slowly phasing out the Milwaukee and Racine programs by allowing current students and their siblings to continue their education through the program. No other students would be allowed to enroll after that.
“We know that having a stable school environment is important for them,” Roys said. “Over time, as these kids… graduate, you are gradually reducing the number of kids who are enrolling in voucher programs. At the same time, you’re increasing the capacity and the quality of the public schools, so that more and more Milwaukee parents will feel excited about their kids attending the public schools in their district.”
Roys was endorsed early on by Wisconsin Education Association Council (WEAC), the state’s largest teacher’s union.
Hong has not laid out a detailed plan for sunsetting the programs, but recently said on Pod Save America that the Milwaukee program would be the last program phased out. 
“Sunsetting that program for Milwaukee, we’re looking at at least the second or third session, so that would be around 2030,” Hong said. “But again, we want to make sure that [Milwaukee Public Schools] is a partner with us and that the families who are in the program, that the education is not disrupted.”
Morgan questioned whether gradual plans could be nondisruptive. 
“I wonder how you practically pull it off, like for all the same reasons that school consolidations in the public school context are really tricky,” Morgan said. “Those schools are not going to stay open. They’re going to hit a tipping point and not be able to operate anymore… It doesn’t work.” 
Public schools advocates expressed concern about the amount of money being funneled out of the public schools by private school choice. 
State Rep. Christian Phelps (D-Eau Claire), who is seeking his second term in office this year, told the Examiner that he is running for reelection this year on a “pro-public education platform.”
“If you drive around Eau Claire, the signs that remain year-round say ‘we love Roosevelt School,’” Phelps said, referring to a school that has faced possible closure. “I don’t know how much longer people can get away with, like sprinkling some crumbs on special ed and doing nothing else in a budget and saying that was a historic increase.” 
Phelps said voters should pay more attention to legislative races because of the Legislature’s role in determining how much the state invests in public schools. Evers has proposed that the state spend more than $7 billion on education, but those calls were rejected by the Republican-led Legislature. 
“We have seen that if the Legislature doesn’t deliver that kind of budget, the governor’s only option is to sign or veto,” Phelps said. 
Holly Sweeney, an Elk Mound School Board member, told the Examiner that her small rural district is doing OK in part because of open enrollment, which allows students who live in neighboring districts including Eau Claire to attend schools in a different district. Sweeney said she is concerned about the amount of money that goes to vouchers in her area — about $120,000 —  which, she said, “doesn’t sound like a lot, but for our little school district, that’s a lot.”
“Our neighboring school district, Chippewa Falls… they have over $3 million going from their schools to voucher schools,” Sweeney said. “That’s something that we’re really concerned about.”

title: Morrisey: WV public school funding formula needs work, spending may not be the answer
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s team laid out his office’s ideas for revamping West Virginia’s school funding formula, a decades-old equation that has been linked to public schools’ dire financial situation.
text:
Sen. Eric Tarr, R-Putnam, and Del. Joe Parsons, R-Jackson, look over a presentation in the Joint Committee on Education on Aug. 9, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s team laid out his office’s ideas for revamping West Virginia’s school funding formula, a decades-old equation that has been linked to public schools’ dire financial situation.
Debate over the funding formula is expected to be a leading topic in the 2027 legislative session.
Morrisey’s office wants to see the formula simplified and more money directed to classrooms, but that doesn’t necessarily mean a hefty financial investment into public schools. 
“The governor has a deep desire to strengthen public education. Everyone should share that desire,” said Curtis Capehart, who represented the governor’s office during a presentation to lawmakers on Sunday at the state Capitol. 
West Virginia uses a seven-step formula to determine how much state funding goes to county school systems based on factors including the number of students enrolled.
State population decline coupled with students leaving public schools for the Hope Scholarship have put many counties in urgent money trouble. The growing number of special education students, which can require costly services, has also impacted schools’ budgets.
Since lawmakers adjourned in March, school officials have sounded alarm bells on worsening school finances, warning multiple counties are headed to insolvency. An additional 5,000 students have left the school system since October, and more school closures are expected.
“The current funding formula is, in a word, complex, relying on multiple steps of intricate calculations that very few people can understand at all,” Capehart told lawmakers. “This inadvertently obscures accountability, prevents everyone, including laborers and taxpayers alike, from readily understanding how funding is out. Any future reform should need to remove complexity in order to increase transparency. 
Morrisey wants to simplify the formula and keep money tied to the student, Capehart said, and the governor’s team believes that the funding formula’s focus on enrollment is one of its better features.
Any reform to the funding formula should be carried out in “a fiscally disciplined manner,” Capehart said. 
“West Virginia ranks near the national average in terms of per pupil spending, but our education results do not. Many states spend substantially less per pupil than West Virginia does, but nonetheless, have significantly better outcomes,” Capehart said. “This demonstrates that injecting more money into the system, simply spending more, is not the answer. “
Financial resources should be focused directly into the classroom, according to Capehart. 
The legislative session concluded in March without lawmakers making any changes to the school funding formula after debate on multiple bills to deal with the issue. Roadblocks often centered on funding concerns; a House bill updating the funding formula would have cost $214 million.
Senate Education Chair Amy Grady, R-Mason. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Capehart’s presentation was the first time lawmakers had heard this list of Morrisey’s education priorities, according to Senate Education Chair Amy Grady, R-Mason.
“Whenever we’re looking at education reform, and we’re looking at how we’re going to change that funding formula, the governor’s office is also a part of that,” Grady said. “We want to make sure that we are all connecting, that we’re all working towards the same goal, instead of you know the two of us working one direction and another one fighting against us.”
Del. Mike Pushkin, D-Kanawha. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. Mike Pushkin, D-Kanawha, raised concerns about the Hope Scholarship, the state’s education voucher program, and its effect on public school finances. 
More than 26,000 students have applied for full funding of the Hope Scholarship for the upcoming school year — the first year the program opens up to all West Virginia students. The program has cost the state of West Virginia an estimated $155 million so far after lawmakers allocated $277 million for the Hope Scholarship to account for any student who uses the program in the 2026-27 school year.  
A $114,000 study paid for by the House recommended that the state put some guardrails on the Hope Scholarship spending — it has a broad list of allowable expenses, including out-of-state schools — in an effort to improve overall school finances.  
“There’s no guardrails there, there’s no regulation there … that, by definition, would take money out of public education,” Pushkin said.
Capehart responded that he “was not here to speak about Hope Scholarship today.” Morrisey has been a staunch supporter of the education voucher program.
Capehart floated other ideas from Morrisey’s office to boost education outcomes in the state, including addressing teacher and staff pay. The National Education Association ranks West Virginia as 47th in the nation for average teacher salary.
“It would be in the long-term interests of the state to create a broad, competitive salary structure that draws more people to these educational professions and rewards,” Capehart said.
